summary: The only flaw with existing NASA’s Earth-observing satellites…Is that they generate massive amounts of vital environmental data, yet raw datasets are often scattered and difficult for everyday citizens and even busy researchers to navigate. Understanding how our planet is changing requires seeing the bigger picture across both time and geography. Seeing this we have chosen and built for the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge. Our web platform transforms complex NASA satellite data into an intuitive, interactive map experience. With a single click on any region, users can investigate specific environmental phenomena, track multi-year historical statistics, and compare local trends side-by-side against other countries or global averages. By making environmental shifts easy to visualize for both children and adults, our platform turns passive observers into informed "trend detectives" who understand the local and global urgency of protecting our home planet. details:
“TerraScope” Project Description

What does it do or how does it work?

TerraScope (terrascope.space) lets anyone pick an Earth science variable and a territory and get an honest answer to four questions: what is changing, where, how fast, and whether the change is statistically significant.

It works on 50 monthly variables, most going back to 1980, from NASA missions and models:

- MERRA-2 reanalysis, at the surface and at 8 pressure levels from 850 to 10 hPa;

- GPM IMERG precipitation;

- MODIS on Terra and Aqua: vegetation indices NDVI and EVI, land surface temperature, land cover, ocean chlorophyll;

- AIRS: air temperature, water vapour, outgoing radiation;

- OMI: tropospheric NO2;

- CERES: clouds, aerosol and sunlight;

- GLDAS: soil moisture, evaporation, runoff, snow.

A territory can be a country, a region, a desert, a sea, a large city, a latitude belt, a point or an area drawn on the map. It can be narrowed to one terrain type using MODIS land cover.

For each territory the tool removes the seasonal cycle and shows the rate of change per decade with its 95% confidence interval. It then runs two independent significance tests: a t-test corrected for autocorrelation and the Mann-Kendall test. Robustness checks follow, and if a trend is not yet significant, the tool says how many years of data it would need.

Maps show where the change is significant, with the false discovery rate controlled across all grid cells. Further views show:

- trends by height in the atmosphere;

- links between variables beyond a shared trend;

- outlooks that are displayed only where a test on past data proved them reliable.

An SI detective (Gemini) chooses which of these tests to run for a visitor's question. Every number it shows comes from our statistics, not from the model.

What benefits does it have?

- Free, no installation, no coding. A student gets a tested answer in seconds from a browser or a phone.

- Honest by design. Every number comes with the test behind it. The tool says "no reliable trend" or "not proven yet" when that is the truth, and shows outlooks only where they beat naive guesses on past data.

- Checked against NASA's own tools. Our area averages are compared with NASA Giovanni (via Harmony) and the NASA POWER API. For example, GPM IMERG over India matches Giovanni with a correlation of 1.000 and a bias of 0.6%.

- Any territory, from a country to a hand-drawn area, narrowed to forests, croplands or cities if needed.

- Two levels. A simple mode asks everyday questions such as "Is it getting hotter?" or "Is the soil drying out?", while a detailed mode shows every test, interval and caveat.

- Open source (MIT), with all methods and data sources cited with DOIs.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We want high school and college students, teachers, journalists and curious citizens to become data detectives: to check claims about a changing planet against NASA data themselves, and to learn the difference between a real trend and noise.

The tool makes visible what statistics usually hides: uncertainty, autocorrelation, and the record length a trend needs before it can be called significant. It also shows the core idea of the challenge, that one process can drive opposite trends. For example, MERRA-2 shows the lower atmosphere warming by about 0.2 °C per decade, while the stratosphere at 10 hPa cools by 0.7 °C per decade, the fingerprint of greenhouse gases.

Local answers make global change personal: a student can look at their own country, city or croplands rather than a global average.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

- Data and APIs:

  - NASA Earthdata (CMR, GES DISC, LP DAAC, OB.DAAC, cloud OPeNDAP), NASA POWER;

  - NASA Harmony and Giovanni, NASA GIBS satellite imagery;

  - Natural Earth boundaries.

- Server: Python 3.14 with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely, DuckDB, xarray, Zarr, h5py and pyhdf for the HDF4 and HDF5 files of NASA products.

- Browser: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, MapLibre GL (map and globe), ECharts, Lucide icons.

- SI inside the product:

  - Google Gemini API for the SI

detective (Gemini 3.8 Flash, with Gemini 2.5 Flash as a fallback);

  - Claude Science, which turned 21 peer-reviewed papers into 19 hypotheses tested through our API.

- Trend by height. One chart shows the troposphere warming and the stratosphere cooling over the same territory: opposite trends from the same cause, exactly the paradox the challenge describes.

- SI as a hypothesis generator, statistics as the judge. Claude Science read the literature and wrote 19 hypotheses about deserts, rainforests, cities, croplands, deltas and polar seas before seeing any result. Our tests then checked each one on two independent periods (1981 to 2003 and 2004 to 2025): 12 were supported, 5 not, 2 contradicted. Failures are reported too, such as Delhi NO2, which rose until 2014 and has fallen since.

- An exhaustive search that guards against itself. 538,479 tests found links on one half of the record and kept only those that repeated on the other half. A control run on time-shifted data estimates how many false links to expect.

- "How many years would it take?" Instead of just saying "not significant", the tool estimates the record length a trend needs to stand out.

- Everyday questions and a drawn area make serious- AI-assisted development. We built TerraScope with Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant:

  - about half of the frontend;

  - part of the backend;

  - part of the data analysis: data loaders, statistical checks and the validation runs.

The team designed the methods, reviewed the code and checked the results. Key numbers were verified independently against NASA Giovanni and the NASA POWER API.

- Quality: pytest, Ruff, Biome, mypy, plus a pre-commit check of every published file.

- Hardware: no special hardware. Everything runs on one small cloud server with 2 CPU cores and 4 GB of memory; the data cube is about 18 GB.

How is your project creative?

 statistics approachable without hiding them.

What factors did your team consider?

- Scientific honesty:

  - autocorrelation in monthly data, using effective sample size;

  - multiple testing, with false discovery rate control on maps and Bonferroni across lags;

  - replication on unseen years;

  - a second independent data source for the same quantity where available.

- Communicating uncertainty: intervals on every rate, verdicts in plain words, robustness flags, outlooks only where validated.

- Data limits: monthly grids of 0.5 to 1 degree (about 50 to 110 km), so city circles and deltas cover only a few cells; records of different length; no seasonal filter yet. We state these limits instead of hiding them.

- Audience and accessibility: a simple mode, English and Russian, a phone layout, keyboard and screen reader support, and fast loading on slower laptops.

- Cost and privacy: the free AI key is protected by request limits and a cache. Visitors can use their own key, which is stored only in their browser.

- Openness and licensing: MIT license, third-party license notices kept in the built site, every data set and method cited with its DOI in docs/REFERENCES.md.
